intro: Geashill, in County Offaly between Tullamore and Portarlington, is a planned estate village laid out by the Digby family around a triangular green. In the middle of that green stands a giant sequoia, planted in 1859 by a reader's account, now the tallest thing in the village. The green is open to everyone, with picnic tables and benches under the trees.
meta_description: The giant sequoia on Geashill village green, Co. Offaly: a Californian giant planted in 1859, by a reader's account, in a Digby estate village.

trees.name: The Geashill Sequoia
trees.age_estimate: about 167 years, planted 1859 by a reader's account
trees.story:
A tree from the mountains of California has stood in the middle of an Irish village green since 1859, by the account of the reader who sent it to us. They add that it was "likely bought as a seedling from Toole's Nursery, Dublin", along with the other trees on the green. Giant sequoias were still a novelty then, a species that had reached these islands as seed only a few years before.

Geashill itself was built to a plan. The Digby family, who owned more than 34,000 acres around it, developed it as an estate village, and in 1837 it had 87 mostly thatched houses set around a triangular green. Edward Digby, the 9th Baron, inherited the estate in 1856 and evicted a large number of families; in the 1860s and 1870s he rebuilt much of the village, and many of the buildings around the green date from then. The sequoia was planted in the middle of those years.

Today it rises above the limes around it, a dark spire with a thick, reddish trunk. The reader calls the green "a lovely spot for young and old alike, with picnic tables and the Geashill Cauldron". Nobody we have read gives its height or girth, so a tape round the trunk would be welcome.
trees.how_to_recognise: The tallest tree on the village green: a dark, conical evergreen with a thick, reddish, fibrous trunk, standing alone on the mown grass between rows of broadleaved limes, a small information board near its foot.

question_meta: The giant sequoia on Geashill village green in County Offaly: when it was planted and how to see it.
question_answer: Geashill's best-known tree is the giant sequoia in the middle of its village green, planted in 1859 by a reader's account, which makes it about 167 years old. It stands on open public grass in the Digby estate village and is free to visit.
question_context: Geashill was developed by the Digby family as a planned estate village around a triangular green; Samuel Lewis counted 87 mostly thatched houses there in 1837. Edward Digby, the 9th Baron, inherited the estate in 1856, evicted many families, and rebuilt much of the village in the 1860s and 1870s. A reader who sent us the tree says the giant sequoia on the green dates from 1859 and was probably bought as a seedling from Toole's Nursery in Dublin, with the other trees planted on the green. It now stands above the limes around it as a dark conical spire with a thick reddish trunk. Its height and girth have not been published. The green has picnic tables and is open to everyone. The sequoia is the species from the Sierra Nevada of California, and it was still new to Irish and British gardens when this one went in. Today it is the tallest tree on the green, standing alone on the mown grass between rows of limes, with a small information board near its foot.
